title: Take Five
pitch: A governed room for humans and agents on WebMCP: the phase you are in is the set of tools the page offers, and every act on the ledger says how we know who did it.
about_excerpt: A governed room for humans and agents on WebMCP: the phase you are in is the set of tools the page offers, and every act on the ledger says how we know who did it. Like Comment Story Updates Take Five — a governed room for humans and agents Live: https://take-five-lw7.pages.dev/ Code: https://github.com/arthapraha/take-five (MIT) Five phases — Open · Commit · Reveal · Ruling · Closed — where the phase the room is in is the set of tools the page offers an agent. Every act lands on an append-only, SHA-256 hash-chained ledger, and every entry records not just what happened, but how well we know who did it . Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP WebMCP's defining move is that the page declares what an agent may do. That makes the page the right place to put a rule — and the natural unit of a rule is not a permission, it is a phase . A governed proceeding is a state machine with sharp edges: you may seal a position now and not open it; you may open it now and not seal a new one; a ruling may be ratified only once and only from Ruling. Every other agent integration expresses that as validation — a tool that exists always and refuses most of the time. WebMCP lets us express it as existence . In Commit, commit_to_round is registered and reveal_in_round is not. Advance, and commit_to_round is gone — unregistered by aborting its AbortSignal , not hidden, not stubbed, not returning an error. Where the browser fires toolchange the badge moves with it; where it does not — ChatGPT's in-app browser has no addEventListener on modelContext — the tool list still changes, because the surface genuinely changed and the render does not depend on the event. The page says which case it is in rather than implying the stronger one. That is a rule an agent cannot argue with, cannot be prompted past, and does not have to be told about. It reads the tools it has. The second fit is subtler and is why this project exists. When an agent rides your browser session, its acts and yours arrive inside the same authenticated session . Existing audit tooling records one agent's actions for its own operator. Nothing records acts between parties in a shared venue — and at the WebMCP door, for the first time, a page can see which path an act arrived by. That is not full attribution. It is more than anyone had, and it is exactly enough to record honestly. How it creates a better user experience By refusing to overstate what it knows. Every ledger entry carries three fields: seat identity , ingress path , and an evidence grade — client-asserted , server-observed , or inherited . The grade is derived from the door the act came through, never passed in by the caller, and the interface never renders an attribution stronger than its grade . An act arriving with no grade is refused outright. You can watch this work rather than take it on faith: The commit-reveal check runs off-page in a Cloudflare Pages Function, so the entry is graded server-observed . When that function is unreachable, the check falls back into the page, grades itself down to client-asserted , and states the reason in its own output. A silent fallback would let a strong label survive a check that never left the browser. Every status chip on the page says what it cannot do. Cross-origin exposure unavailable in this browser? The chip says so, and no cross-org claim is made. Verification runs in your browser, over the whole chain, and can fail: the test suite includes altered content, a severed link, and the rehash-one-entry repair attempt that still breaks every entry after it. A verifier that cannot fail proves nothing. The result is an interface a sceptical person can use as an instrument instead of as a claim. That is the better experience: not more confidence, but confidence you can check. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before Share a venue and leave a record neither party controls. Before WebMCP, an agent acting on a web app was indistinguishable from its human at the door — the session was the identity, and the page had no view of the route. Take Five demonstrates three things that become possible when the page declares the surface: An agent cannot read the room without leaving a mark. The read tools are themselves acts. Ask the agent to read the ledger and the read appears on the ledger , graded and attributed, between the two calls it made. The ask and the answer stay separate. ratify_ruling is registered only in Ruling and cannot ratify . It raises a request and blocks on a human. Two entries land, never one — the ask is the agent's, through the WebMCP door; the answer is the host's, through the UI door. Collapsing them would credit an agent with a decision it only asked for. A declined ratification stays on the chain permanently. The division of labour is legible on the record, not just in the prose: the human sets the question, advances the phases and rules; the agent acts through the tools; the chain records both, each through its own door. Neither party can perform the other's acts without the ledger saying which door it came through. A claim can cross an organisational boundary and stay labelled as borrowed. A separate origin calls into the room via exposedTo , and the room records the claim verbatim , names the origin that made it, and carries a SHA-256 over the claim bytes that anyone can recompute — graded inherited : we did not witness this, we carried it; trust it exactly as far as you trust that origin. The digest is on the ledger row, so a reader watching the demo can check the room's arithmetic without being given anything but the picture. Cross-organisation tool access here is not ambient. The room delegates the tools Permissions Policy to a named frame, and exposedTo allowlists a named origin. Two independent gates, both auditable, neither of them ours. Produced live on 31 August in Chrome 151 behind the WebMCP testing flags, and again on 2 September in Chrome 152 on the deployed build — with a local agent attached to the same page at the same time, which was never offered the partner's tool. The inherited row is a thing that happens, not a row we describe. Bring your own agent. The page publishes its tools through WebMCP; a small local bridge in this repository lets any MCP client outside the browser call exactly the tools the page would show a riding agent — and nothing else. We built our own side panel, Take Five Agent , to show it: type a prompt, and an agent on your machine, calling a model you choose — in our run, glm-5.3 through a local Ollama client to Ollama's cloud — calls the page's own read_ledger , and the call lands on the chain as a tool: row through the WebMCP door, chained to a bridge_opened row that names the door it came through. The agent is not in the browser and not ours to vouch for; the row says so. video_transcript_excerpt: This is Take 5, a governed room where humans and agents act together. Five phases, and the phase you're in is the set of tools the page offers an agent. Where the browser can't do something, the page says so rather than pretending. Watch for it. Everything here sits behind document.modelcontext. The agent sees five read-only tools. Watch what happens when it uses one. The read itself lands on the chain. The agent cannot look at this room without leaving a mark. We are in commit. The agent can seal a position without disclosing it. The room stores only the hash of the position and a nonce. And commit around exists only in this phase. Advance, and it is gone. Not hidden, unregistered. Reveal in round has taken its place. That list is the agent's actual surface, not a menu we are drawing next to it. Or bring your own agent. Ours runs outside the browser, asks the page for its tools, and the chain records the call. The reveal recomputes the digest off page in a Cloudflare function, so this entry is graded server observed. If that function is unreachable, the check falls back into the page, grades itself down to client asserted, and says why in its own output. A silent fallback would let a strong label survive a check that never left the browser. Ratify.underscore.ruling cannot ratify. It raises a request and blocks on a human. The human sets the question and rules. The agent acts through the tools. The chain records both, each through its own door. Two entries land, never one. The ask is the agent's, the answer the host's. A refusal stays on the chain permanently. Now the part we would rather not have found. Web MCP's primitive for a human gate, request user interaction, does not exist. Not in in polyfill, not in flagged Chrome, not in chat GPT's browser. So, the room uses its own ratified dialogue and records what pressed it. This click was a person's and the row says the page cannot tell that from an agent driving the browser. A page cannot require a human today. Anything claiming to describe the convention, not a control. And when a claim arrives from another organization, the room records it verbatim, names the origin that made it, and hashes what it was given, then grades it inherited. We did not see this happen. We carried it. Trust it exactly as far as you trust that origin. Every hash recomputed, every link checked in your browser. Nothing here asks you to take the chain on trust. That is the product, not certainty about who acted, but an honest record of how well we know.

live_observation.first_impression: A room-and-chain interface presents a governed proceeding with the current phase, question, agent tools, seats, evidence grades, and chain controls.
live_observation.after_state: The phase advanced and the control changed to Advance to Ruling, while the room and chain panels remained visible.
live_observation.notes: The phase transition was directly observable; Verify chain and partner attestation controls were also present.
